chicken-thigh-baked-or-broiled-skin-eate.title: Chicken thigh, baked or broiled, skin eaten, from pre‑cooked (830)

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is dark meat that contains more fat than white meat. When baked or broiled with the skin left on, the skin becomes crispy while the meat stays juicy. The pre‑cooked code (830) indicates that the product has already undergone heat treatment and is ready to eat after reheating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs are rich in iron and zinc, minerals important for immune function.
Leaving the skin on adds flavor and a pleasant crunchy texture.
Dark meat contains more monounsaturated fats than white meat.
Pre‑cooked items are widely used in cafeterias and catering to speed up service.
Thighs can be marinated in a variety of sauces—from soy‑ginger to honey‑mustard.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in meat is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: Zinc and B‑vitamins contribute to healthy skin and hair.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Fats in the skin provide lasting satiety and a quick energy source.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Thighs with skin contain higher levels of saturated fat, so intake should be moderated for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper reheating of pre‑cooked products can allow bacterial growth.

items.title: Chicken meat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Marinated versions often contain added salt, increasing sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat chicken thighs in the oven, microwave, or skillet. They work well in salads, pastas, rice dishes, and as a filling for sandwiches and wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pre‑cooked thighs refrigerated at ≤ 4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at -18 °C. Ensure the product is heated through before consumption.

cream-of-wheat-regular-or-quick-made-wit.title: Cream of Wheat, regular or quick, made with water, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Cream of Wheat is a finely milled wheat farina, available in regular and quick‑cooking versions. When prepared with water and a splash of fat (oil or butter) it becomes a smooth, creamy breakfast porridge.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream of Wheat was introduced in the United States in 1893 and quickly became a staple breakfast.
The quick‑cooking version uses pre‑treated grains that cook in 1–2 minutes.
It is often used in infant and toddler diets because of its soft texture and neutral flavor.
In the U.S. it is commonly served with honey, cinnamon, berries, or nuts.
The wheat is fortified with iron and B‑vitamins.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Fortified wheat provides iron that supports normal blood formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin and niacin help carbohydrate metabolism and maintain nervous system health.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The fine texture makes the porridge gentle on the stomach, suitable for people with digestive sensitivities.

items.title: Low in fiber
items.content: Beneficial for low‑fiber diets, such as those required after certain gastrointestinal procedures.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates provide rapid energy, and added fat prolongs satiety.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Individuals with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The porridge can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Added fat increases calories
items.content: Adding oil or butter raises the caloric content; those watching weight should account for it.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: For those needing high dietary fiber, Cream of Wheat alone may be insufficient.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine 1 cup of water with ¼ cup of dry farina, bring to a boil, reduce heat and simmer 2–5 minutes (quick version 1–2 minutes). Stir in 1–2 teaspoons of oil or butter, sweetener, fruit, nuts, or spices to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry farina in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. After opening, use within 6 months. Moisture can cause clumping and spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Dry whole milk is a dehydrated dairy product obtained by evaporating water from whole cow’s milk. When reconstituted with water, it reproduces the properties of regular whole milk, including taste, nutrients, and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry milk is easy to store and transport because it does not require refrigeration.
Reconstituted dry milk is widely used in the food industry for ice cream, confectionery, and dry mixes.
The fat content in whole dry milk preserves a creamy mouthfeel after reconstitution.
Dry milk has been a staple for military rations and expeditions due to its long shelf life.
When properly reconstituted, dry milk is virtually indistinguishable in flavor from fresh whole milk.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: Whole dry milk provides a high amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Reconstituted milk contains complete milk protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Vitamin D content
items.content: Many dry milks are fortified with vitamin D, which aids calcium absorption.

items.title: Convenience and cost‑effectiveness
items.content: Provides whole milk without the need for fresh storage, saving space and money.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Dry milk contains lactose, so it should be avoided by people with lactose intolerance or replaced with lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Whole dry milk has a relatively high fat level, which may be unsuitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Shelf life after reconstitution
items.content: Reconstituted milk must be kept refrigerated and consumed within a few days.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: To reconstitute, dissolve 1 part dry milk in 4–5 parts cold water, stirring until smooth. The resulting milk can be drunk, used in cooking, added to sauces, cereals, baked goods, and infant formulas.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry milk in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. After reconstitution, keep the milk refrigerated and use within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Jalapeno is a variety of hot pepper (Capsicum annuum) originating from Mexico. It is bright green, 5–10 cm long, and has a moderate heat level of about 2 500–8 000 Scoville units. Jalapenos are used fresh, as well as pickled, dried, and smoked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Jalapenos were domesticated by indigenous peoples more than 6 000 years ago.
The capsaicin content makes them a popular ingredient for boosting metabolism.
In the United States, jalapeno is the most popular fresh hot pepper.
There are green (young) and red (ripe) jalapenos; the ripe ones are sweeter and hotter.
Eating a raw jalapeno can cause a burning sensation that lasts from a few minutes up to an hour.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Jalapenos provide over 100 % of the daily value of vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin has anti‑inflammatory and analgesic effects and may help increase metabolic rate.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in jalapenos converts to vitamin A, important for vision and skin health.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A medium jalapeno contains fewer than 5 kcal, making it a great addition to calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: People with sensitivity to spicy foods may experience heartburn or gastric irritation after eating jalapenos.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may develop allergic reactions to capsaicin or other pepper compounds.

items.title: Caution with children
items.content: Due to its heat, raw jalapeno is not recommended for young children.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Capsaicin can enhance the effects of certain anticoagulants; consult a healthcare professional if you take such medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jalapenos can be eaten fresh in salads, salsas, guacamole, and added to sauces, marinades, and soups. They are often pickled in vinegar or brine, dried and ground into powder. To reduce heat, remove the seeds and membranes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh jalapenos in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel, for 1‑2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze them whole or sliced. Dried and pickled jalapenos keep in a sealed jar in a cool, dark place.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese‑flavored potato chips are thin slices of potato that are fried or baked until crisp and then coated with a savory cheese seasoning. They have a rich, creamy‑cheese taste, a hint of salt, and a satisfying crunch, making them a popular snack worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheesy flavor is usually achieved with a blend of dried dairy powders, such as cheddar, parmesan, and flavor enhancers.
Mass production of cheese‑flavored chips began in the early 1970s in the United States.
There are more than 20 cheese seasoning variants: cheddar, parmesan, blue cheese, and even spicy chipotle‑cheese blends.
Chips can be prepared by deep‑frying or by hot‑air ovens, which reduces fat content.
In some markets the chips are sold in single‑serve packets to preserve crunch and aroma longer.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The carbohydrates in potato chips rapidly replenish glycogen stores for active muscles.

items.title: Calcium from cheese seasoning
items.content: Cheese powders can provide a modest amount of calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of vitamin B6, and cheese adds small amounts of B12.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of salty and creamy flavors can increase feelings of fullness and help curb overeating.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese‑flavored chips often contain a lot of salt, which may raise blood pressure if eaten frequently.

items.title: High fat levels
items.content: Traditional deep‑frying makes them calorie‑dense and rich in saturated fats.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese seasonings can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergies.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oils are used, trans fats may form, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the chips straight from the bag, toss them into salads, use as a crunchy topping for soups, or incorporate them into dishes like casseroles. Opt for versions with moderate salt and no artificial additives for a healthier choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in an airtight bag or container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For extended freshness, store them in the refrigerator to maintain crunch and prevent fat oxidation.
